venues.name: Four Seasons Hotel Buenos Aires
venues.note: A modern tower and a restored 1916 Belle Époque mansion (La Mansión) side by side in Recoleta, the city's most complete grand hotel, and its most decorated.

venues.name: Palacio Duhau, Park Hyatt Buenos Aires
venues.note: A 1930s French-style palace joined to a modern wing by an art-lined garden tunnel, terraced gardens, a cheese room and quietly impeccable Recoleta grandeur.

venues.name: Alvear Palace Hotel
venues.note: The 1932 gilded grande dame of Avenida Alvear, Louis XV and XVI furnishings, white-gloved butlers and a century of Argentine high-society ceremony.
credentials: The Leading Hotels of the World

venues.name: Faena Hotel Buenos Aires
venues.note: Philippe Starck's theatrical red-and-white fantasy inside a converted 1902 grain mill, unicorn statues, a cabaret hall and pure Argentine drama on the docks.

venues.name: Casa Lucía
venues.note: A 1929 Bencich-family building on Avenida Santa Fe reborn as a warm, art-filled modern house, timber, brass and a rooftop pool over the city.
credentials: Small Luxury Hotels of the World

venues.name: Palacio Duhau, Park Hyatt (Palacio-wing suites)
venues.note: The palace-wing suites of the Duhau, grand proportions, French mouldings and garden or Avenida Alvear views, with the full Park Hyatt service.

venues.name: Four Seasons Buenos Aires, La Mansión suites
venues.note: The seven suites within the restored 1916 mansion, the most exclusive rooms in the city, with private grandeur and the full Four Seasons hand.

venues.name: Alvear Icon Hotel
venues.note: The Alvear group's sleek modern tower on the Puerto Madero waterfront, high floors, river and city views and a rooftop pool and spa.
credentials: Alvear maison (sister to The Leading Hotels of the World Alvear Palace)

venues.name: Hotel Madero
venues.note: A polished contemporary hotel on the Puerto Madero docks, a rooftop pool, a spa and a quiet, well-run calm a short walk from the old town.

venues.name: Aramburu
venues.note: Gonzalo Aramburu's precise, artful tasting menu, the highest gastronomic reference in the country, and Argentina's only two-Michelin-star table.

venues.name: Don Julio
venues.note: Pablo Rivero's parrilla, the definitive Argentine steakhouse, No. 1 in all of Latin America and a one-star table where the grill is treated as an art.

venues.name: Trescha
venues.note: Tomás Treschanski's 14-course counter for just ten diners, a young, virtuosic kitchen and the city's most exciting fine-dining seat.
credentials: Latin America's 50 Best Restaurants 2024, No. 33 (Highest New Entry)

venues.name: Crizia
venues.note: Gabriel Oggero's oyster bar and seafood-driven kitchen in a leafy Palermo townhouse, the newest of the city's Michelin stars.

venues.name: El Preferido de Palermo
venues.note: A restored 1952 corner bodegón reborn under the Don Julio family, Spanish-Argentine classics, house-cured hams and a joyful, buzzing room.

venues.name: Mishiguene
venues.note: Tomás Kalika's reimagining of Jewish diaspora cooking, pastrami, babka and shakshuka elevated to a celebrated, soulful fine-dining table.

venues.name: Niño Gordo
venues.note: A neon-lit, theatrical 'Asian parrilla', Argentine fire cooking crossed with Southeast and East Asian flavours, loud and hugely fun.

venues.name: Julia
venues.note: A tiny, produce-obsessed neighbourhood kitchen, a short, changing menu of quietly brilliant contemporary cooking from chef Julio Martín Báez.

venues.name: Gran Dabbang
venues.note: Mariano Ramón's tiny, riotous storefront where Indian and Southeast Asian spice meets Argentine produce, one of the most loved kitchens in the city.

venues.name: Anchoíta
venues.note: A farm-to-table kitchen with its own organic plot, Guaraní-inspired sharing plates, house charcuterie, river fish and superb pasta.

venues.name: Sacro
venues.note: Buenos Aires' most ambitious plant-based kitchen, gourmet vegan cooking, a serious cocktail list and a sleek, grown-up room.

venues.name: Elena
venues.note: The Four Seasons' dry-aging steakhouse and all-day room, polished Argentine grilling and one of the best Sunday brunches in the city.
credentials: Within Four Seasons Hotel Buenos Aires

venues.name: Chila
venues.note: A long-standing fine-dining room on the Puerto Madero docks, a tasting-menu celebration of Argentina's regions and its wines.

venues.name: Anafe
venues.note: A small, chef-led corner bistro celebrated for inventive, produce-driven cooking at an accessible price.

venues.name: Café Tortoni
venues.note: The city's most storied café since 1858, stained glass, marble and mirrors, and the ghosts of Borges and Gardel over coffee and churros.
credentials: Historic landmark (est. 1858); a founding member of the world's historic cafés

venues.name: El Cuartito
venues.note: A beloved 1934 pizzeria plastered in football and boxing memorabilia, thick porteño pizza and fugazzeta the way the city has always eaten it.
credentials: Historic landmark (est. 1934); a Buenos Aires institution

venues.name: La Recoleta Cemetery
venues.note: A hushed marble city of the dead where 4,691 above-ground vaults, Evita Perón's among them, line avenues of angels and domes. A private guide turns the sprawl into an hour of storytelling that even restless teenagers fall quiet for; go early, before the coach groups arrive.

venues.name: Teatro Colón
venues.note: Argentina's grand opera house, ranked among the world's finest for acoustics, Pavarotti said its perfection made him nervous. A box for the evening, or a private daytime tour of the golden horseshoe auditorium and marble Salón Dorado, is the city at its most refined.
credentials: Rated among the world's top three opera houses for acoustics by National Geographic

venues.name: Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes
venues.note: The finest art collection in Latin America, Goya, Rembrandt, Rodin, Monet, Van Gogh and the deepest holding of Argentine masters, all with free entry. A civilised, air-conditioned hour between lunch and the cemetery, easily paced for grandparents.

venues.name: Plaza de Mayo
venues.note: The historic heart of the nation, framed by the pink Casa Rosada, the colonial Cabildo and the Cathedral, the square where Evita addressed the masses and the Mothers still march on Thursdays. A guide unpacks two centuries of Argentine drama in one walkable block.

venues.name: Casa Rosada
venues.note: The rose-pink presidential palace whose famous balcony framed Evita, and, for many, the ghost of the Broadway song. Free weekend tours reveal the halls of power, or simply admire the facade from the plaza on a private history walk.

venues.name: Buenos Aires Metropolitan Cathedral
venues.note: Behind a Greek-temple facade lies the country's principal church, where Jorge Bergoglio said mass before becoming Pope Francis, and where General San Martín's remains rest under permanent guard. Quietly moving even for non-Catholic visitors.

venues.name: El Ateneo Grand Splendid
venues.note: A 1919 theatre, frescoed ceiling, crimson stage curtain, opera boxes intact, reborn as a bookshop where you browse novels from the old balcony seats. A magical, unhurried stop the whole family enjoys, coffee served on the former stage.
credentials: Named the world's most beautiful bookstore by National Geographic (2019)

venues.name: Avenida 9 de Julio & the Obelisco
venues.note: The city's Champs-Élysées and Eiffel Tower in one, reputedly the world's widest avenue, crowned by the 67-metre Obelisco. Best seen at dusk from a private car as the traffic-light rivers begin to glow.

venues.name: Don Julio
venues.note: The parrilla that turned the Argentine steak into world-class theatre, Angus and Hereford dry-aged in its own butchery, poured with a wall of Malbec. Book weeks ahead and let the maître d' arrange a private table; the kitchen handles vegetarians and grilled-vegetable feasts with real care when told in advance.

venues.name: San Telmo Sunday Market
venues.note: Every Sunday, Defensa Street becomes ten blocks of antiques, silver, leather and buskers, converging on cobbled Plaza Dorrego where couples still dance tango as the light fades. A guide keeps the crowd manageable and steers you to the genuine dealers, not the trinket stalls.

venues.name: Caminito & La Boca
venues.note: The postcard lane of tin houses painted in leftover shipyard colours, where tango was born among Genoese dockworkers. Best enjoyed mid-morning with a private guide who keeps you within the safe tourist blocks and adds the real immigrant history behind the pretty facades.

venues.name: Puente de la Mujer & Puerto Madero
venues.note: Calatrava's white 'Woman's Bridge', a stylised tango dancer in steel, arcs over the old docks, now the city's polished riverside quarter of glass towers and terraced restaurants. An easy, flat evening stroll before a waterside dinner, safe and pram-friendly.

venues.name: MALBA (Museo de Arte Latinoamericano)
venues.note: Costantini's private collection turned public: Frida Kahlo, Diego Rivera, Tarsila do Amaral and the giants of Latin American modernism in a cool, light-filled building. Compact enough for an afternoon, with an excellent café for a pause.

venues.name: Bosques de Palermo (Parque Tres de Febrero)
venues.note: The city's green lungs, 400 hectares of lakes, jacaranda and rowing boats, laid out by landscape master Carlos Thays. A gentle morning for multi-generational groups: pedal boats for the children, shaded benches for the elders.

venues.name: El Rosedal (Palermo Rose Garden)
venues.note: More than 8,000 roses across 90-odd species, pergolas and a poets' garden inside the Bosques, the park's most beloved corner and a florid backdrop for family photographs. Free, serene, and at its peak in the southern spring (October–November).
credentials: Protected as part of Buenos Aires' Cultural Heritage

venues.name: Jardín Japonés
venues.note: One of the largest Japanese gardens outside Japan, gifted for a royal visit, koi ponds, red bridges, a teahouse and clipped calm minutes from the city rush. A restful, veg-friendly lunch stop that particularly delights grandparents.

venues.name: Basílica de Nuestra Señora del Pilar
venues.note: The whitewashed colonial jewel beside the cemetery, its original 18th-century Peruvian silver altars still intact, with a small cloister museum upstairs. A five-minute, deeply atmospheric pairing with a Recoleta cemetery visit.

venues.name: Floralis Genérica
venues.note: A 20-metre steel-and-aluminium flower that opens its petals at dawn and closes them at dusk, mirrored in a reflecting pool, the city's modern icon. A free, photogenic pause on the way between the Fine Arts museum and the law faculty.

venues.name: Centro Cultural Recoleta
venues.note: A former convent turned contemporary-arts complex, rotating exhibitions, design shows and a rooftop that catches the afternoon light, right beside the cemetery and basilica. A cool, unhurried counterpoint to the neighbourhood's grand history.

venues.name: Rojo Tango at Faena
venues.note: Tango's most exclusive show: a red-velvet cabaret for barely a hundred guests inside Philippe Starck's Faena Hotel, so close you feel the bandoneón. The discreet, luxurious choice for couples and small parties who want spectacle without a tourist crowd.

venues.name: Café de los Angelitos tango show
venues.note: A grand dinner-and-show in an 1890 café once frequented by Carlos Gardel himself, the most complete traditional tango experience, with a full orchestra and a Malbec-paired menu. Vegetarian courses available on request; ideal for a first, immersive night of tango.

venues.name: Café Tortoni
venues.note: The city's oldest café, founded in 1858, where Borges and Gardel once sat beneath stained glass and marble columns. A living relic, order a submarino (hot milk with a bar of chocolate) and soak up a slower Buenos Aires.
credentials: Historic landmark (est. 1858); a founding member of the world's historic cafés

venues.name: Argentine Open Polo Championship (Palermo)
venues.note: The world's most prestigious polo tournament, played each November–December at the 'Cathedral of Polo' since 1928, where 40-goal teams draw crowds of 30,000. Box seats, an asado and a chilled Malbec make it the season's grand social occasion for Indian polo enthusiasts.

venues.name: Colonia del Sacramento day trip (Uruguay)
venues.note: A one-hour fast ferry across the Río de la Plata to Uruguay's oldest town, cobbled Portuguese-Spanish lanes, a lighthouse and riverside cafés, walkable in an afternoon. Passports and a private transfer make for an effortless second-country stamp.

venues.name: Tigre Delta
venues.note: An hour north, the Paraná fans into a maze of green islands, stilt houses and rowing clubs best explored by private launch, with the Puerto de Frutos market to browse afterwards. A cooling, scenic day on the water for all ages.

venues.name: El Zanjón de Granados
venues.note: Beneath an 1830 mansion lies a restored labyrinth of brick tunnels and cisterns tracing 400 years of the city's foundations, a private, atmospheric hour few tourists know. The most rewarding hidden gem in San Telmo.

venues.name: Museo Nacional de Arte Decorativo (Palacio Errázuriz)
venues.note: A French Beaux-Arts palace by the architect of Buenos Aires' grandest mansions, its rooms hung with El Greco, Manet and Rodin, the only such house that opens regularly to the public. A jewel-box afternoon for lovers of design and la belle époque.

venues.name: Palacio Paz (Círculo Militar)
venues.note: The largest private house ever built in Argentina, 140 rooms of Louvre-inspired grandeur, a soaring domed rotunda and marble halls, now open by guided tour. Occasional evening tours pair the palace with a lyrical concert or wine tasting.

venues.name: Fundación Proa
venues.note: La Boca's serious side: a sleek glass-and-steel contemporary art centre with world-class temporary shows and a rooftop café overlooking the Riachuelo. A refined, safe anchor before or after the colourful chaos of Caminito.

venues.name: Palermo Soho
venues.note: The city's most stylish quarter, independent designers, leather ateliers, art galleries and pavement cafés radiating from leafy Plaza Serrano. The place to shop for one-off pieces and graze between boutiques; a personal shopper smooths the way.

venues.name: Palermo Hollywood
venues.note: Palermo's cooler, more grown-up cousin, threaded with acclaimed restaurants, cocktail bars and cinema-studio history, coming alive after 10pm as Argentines do. Ideal for a long, late dinner and a nightcap without the backpacker throng.

venues.name: Vinoteca at Palacio Duhau – Park Hyatt
venues.note: A cellar of 500-plus labels inside a restored palace, where a sommelier walks you through blind Malbec flights paired with the kitchen's small plates. A discreet, luxurious way to learn Argentine wine without leaving the city.

venues.name: Puerta cerrada (closed-door) dinner
venues.note: Argentina's intimate answer to fine dining, a home turned private restaurant seating a handful of guests, with sommelier hosts and a multi-course, wine-paired menu. Bookable exclusively for your party, and happy to build a vegetarian tasting when asked.

venues.name: Avenida de Mayo & Palacio Barolo
venues.note: The stately Parisian boulevard linking the Casa Rosada to Congress, crowned by the Palacio Barolo, a 1923 tower designed as a stone homage to Dante's Divine Comedy, with a lighthouse-topped viewpoint. A guided climb rewards you with one of the city's best panoramas.

venues.name: Congreso de la Nación
venues.note: The green-domed national Congress closing Avenida de Mayo, a Greco-Roman monument to Argentine democracy with free guided tours of its chambers and library. A grand architectural bookend to a historic-centre walk.

venues.name: Galerías Pacífico
venues.note: A belle-époque shopping arcade under a frescoed cupola painted by Argentina's leading muralists, luxury boutiques below fine art above, on pedestrian Calle Florida. Elegant browsing and a cultural centre make it a rainy-afternoon refuge.

venues.name: Milonga at Salón Canning / La Catedral
venues.note: Not a show but the real thing, a social dance hall where porteños of every age dance tango until dawn, from grand parquet salons to bohemian converted warehouses. A guide or private teacher lets you watch (or step in) with the etiquette right.

venues.name: Feria de Mataderos
venues.note: A weekend fair on the city's edge where gauchos ride, folk musicians play and the pampas comes to town, crafts, empanadas and a horseback skill game called the sortija. The most authentic, least touristy folk experience in Buenos Aires, best reached by private car.

venues.name: Museo Evita
venues.note: Set in a 1920s mansion Evita once ran as a shelter, this intimate museum traces her extraordinary rise through gowns, film and photographs. Essential context for anyone moved by her story at Recoleta, and easily paired with a Palermo lunch.

venues.name: Planetario Galileo Galilei
venues.note: A striking modernist sphere on three arches inside the Bosques, with immersive dome shows and lakeside lawns around it. A fun, air-conditioned hour for families with children, and a photogenic landmark at dusk.

venues.name: Chacarita's La Chacra & the parrilla circuit
venues.note: Beyond Don Julio, a private steak-and-wine crawl through the city's best asadores, La Cabrera, Parrilla Peña, Niño Gordo, is a delicious education in cuts, chimichurri and provoleta. A knowledgeable guide secures the tables and translates the grill.

venues.name: Tres Monos
venues.note: A high-energy, no-menu cocktail den with a social conscience, the highest-ranked bar in South America and a genuine world-beater.

venues.name: CoChinChina
venues.note: Inés de los Santos's theatrical bar where Vietnam and France meet an Argentine accent, polished, glamorous and one of the world's best.

venues.name: Florería Atlántico
venues.note: A flower shop and wine cellar hiding a legendary basement bar, the pioneer of the modern Buenos Aires scene, and a former World's No. 1.
credentials: Rémy Martin Legend Award (pioneer of the scene)

venues.name: Presidente Bar
venues.note: The grand end of Buenos Aires cocktail culture, chandeliers over a long bar, a winter garden and a library-styled private room.

venues.name: Trade Sky Bar
venues.note: A Gatsby-styled rooftop with 360-degree views over the Obelisk, Puerto Madero and downtown, the city's most glamorous high-up drink.

venues.name: Nicky Harrison
venues.note: A Prohibition-era speakeasy hidden behind a sushi counter, password entry, live jazz and a 1920s-with-an-Argentine-twist theatre.
credentials: Widely cited Buenos Aires speakeasy (goop; press)

venues.name: L'Orangerie (Alvear Palace)
venues.note: The Alvear Palace's glass-roofed salon, crystal chandeliers, monogrammed china and the most ceremonial afternoon tea or aperitif in the city.
credentials: Within Alvear Palace Hotel, The Leading Hotels of the World

venues.name: Piano Nobile / Oak Bar (Palacio Duhau)
venues.note: The Park Hyatt palace's clubby wood-panelled bar and garden terrace, impeccable classics, a whisky and cognac library and quiet Recoleta calm.
credentials: Within Palacio Duhau, Park Hyatt (MICHELIN Key, 2025)
